No sweat even with these kind of patterns: :::{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} ![](./img/eigen_face.png){width="300pt" fig-align="center"} ::: ::: ::: :::{.vspace style="--space: -40px"} :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - Other than cats & dogs, it's much more useful to identify - Email spams [{{< fa envelope >}}]{.blue} - Frauds in banking systems [{{< fa triangle-exclamation >}}]{.orange} - Diseases in health care system [{{< fa stethoscope >}}]{.green} ... ::: ::: ::: ## Motivation & Introduction :::{.columns} :::{.column width="60%"} :::{style="font-size: 70%"} - [**Machine Learning (ML):**]{.blue} a branch of [**AI**]{.red} focuses on enabling **computers / machines** to imitate the way that **humans** learn. ![](https://hassothea.github.io/files/figs/ML_branches.png){ width="450px" fig-align="center"} ::: ::: :::{.column width="40%"} :::{style="font-size: 70%" .incremental .fragment} There are 3 main branches: :::{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} - [**Supervised Learning:**]{.red} use labeled data ($X$,Y) and aims at predicting $y$ using $X$. - [**Unsupervised Learning:**]{.blue} use unlabeled data $X$ for clustering and reducing the dimension of $X$. - [**Reinforcement Learning:**]{.orange} agents (models) learn to complete tasks by interacting with an env. to maximize rewards. ::: ::: ::: ::: ```{python} # path = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hassothea/MLcourses/main/data/" path = './data/' ``` # Naive Bayes Classifier (NBC) {background-color="#15797A"} ## General notation :::{.columns} :::{.column width="60%"} :::{style="font-size: 78%"} - Consider Email spam dataset [{{< fa envelope >}}]{.blue}: ```{python} #| code-line-numbers: "|1|2|3|4" #| code-fold: false #| output-location: fragment import pandas as pd # Load package 'pandas' and call it 'pd' spam = pd.read_csv(path + "spam.txt", sep=" ") # 'path' in your machine spam = spam.drop(columns=["Id"]) spam.iloc[:3,[0,2,3,-1]] ``` - Input ($\text{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$) & target ($\text{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n$): [$$\text{X}=\begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1} & x_{1,2} & \dots & x_{1,d}\\ {\color{blue}{x_{2,1}}} & {\color{blue}{x_{2,2}}} & \dots & {\color{blue}{x_{2,d}}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ x_{n,1} & x_{n,2} & \dots & x_{n,d} \end{pmatrix}\quad \&\quad \text{y}=\begin{pmatrix} y_{1}\\ {\color{blue}{y_{2}}}\\ \vdots\\ y_{n}\end{pmatrix}$$]{style="font-size: 85%"} ::: ::: :::{.column width="40%"} :::{style="font-size: 73%" .fragment} - Example: an **input**: ${\color{blue}{\text{x}_i}}=({\color{blue}{x_{i1}}},{\color{blue}{x_{i2}}},\dots, {\color{blue}{x_{id}}})$: `Bag of words` of email $i$. :::{.incremental .vspace style="--space: -20px"} - **Target** ${\color{blue}{y_i}}\in\{1,0\}$ with
{$1:$ [spam]{.light-red}, $0:$ [nonspam]{.green}}. - If $y_i$ are qualitative, the problem is called [**Classification**]{.blue}. - If $y_i$ are quantitative, the problem is called [**Regression**]{.red}. - Example: [**Classify**]{.blue} if an email is a [spam]{.light-red} or not. ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Binary NBC :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 78%"} - Data shape: `{python} spam.shape`. - Total [missing]{.light-red} values: `{python} int(spam.isna().sum().sum())`. - Total [duplicated rows]{.light-red} `{python} int(spam.duplicated().sum())`. - After removing [duplicates]{.light-red}: ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: center import seaborn as sns import matplotlib.pyplot as plt sns.set(style="whitegrid") _, ax = plt.subplots(1,1,figsize=(3.5,2)) spam.drop_duplicates(inplace=True) sns.countplot( data=spam, x="type", hue="type", stat="percent") ax.set_title("Barplot of Email Type") ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], fmt="%.2f", ) ax.bar_label(ax.containers[1], fmt="%.2f") plt.show() ``` ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - As a human, how would you predict if an email is a spam or not just by looking at its features? - [**Main principal of Binary NBC:**]{.blue} Look at each [**feature marginally**]{.light-blue}, then [**combine the information**]{.light-red} to produce the class probability. - This can be accomplished using [**Bayesian Theorem**]{.blue} + some [**assumption**]{.light-red}. ::: ::: ::: --- ### Model Motivation :::{style="font-size:80%" .incremental} - Given an email (input) $\text{x}_i=(0, 0.64,\dots,278)\in\mathbb{R}^{57}$, how would you guess its type $y_i$? - 🔑 [**The most important quantity**]{.green} in (binary) classification: [$$\boxed{\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1|X=\text{x}_i)}.}$$ [**Interpretation:** Given $\text{x}_i$, how likely that it is in class 1 (spam)?]{.blue}]{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} - [**Decision rule:**]{.blue} [$$\boxed{\text{ Email x}_i\text{ is a spam }\Leftrightarrow\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1|X=\text{x}_i)}\geq 0.5.}$$]{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} - From now, building a **classifier** is trying to estimate this chance [$$\boxed{\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1|X=\text{x}_i)}.}$$]{.vspace style="--space: -15px"} ::: --- ### Recall Bayes's Theorem ::: {.callout-tip} ### Bayes's Theorem :::{.columns} :::{.column width="70%"} For any two events $O,H$ with $\mathbb{P}(O)\times\mathbb{P}(H)>0,$ \begin{equation}\overbrace{\mathbb{P}(H|O)}^{\text{Posterior}}=\frac{\overbrace{\mathbb{P}(O|H)}^{\text{Likelihood}}\times\overbrace{\mathbb{P}(H)}^{\text{Prior}}}{\underbrace{\mathbb{P}(O)}_{\text{Marginal}}}.\end{equation} :::{style="font-size: 85%"} - $\mathbb{P}(H)$: Prior belief of having hypothesis $H$. - $\mathbb{P}(O|H)$: If $H$ is true, how likely for $O$ to be observed? - $\mathbb{P}(H|O)$: If $O$ is observed, how likely for $H$ to be true? - $\mathbb{P}(O)$: How likely for $O$ to be observed in general? ::: ::: :::{.column width="30%"} ![](./img/diagram.png){width="180"} :::{.vspace style='--space: -20px'} [![](./img/Thomas.png){width="170"}](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bayes){target="_blank"} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### Model Setting :::{style="font-size:85%" .incremental} - Bayes's theorem implies: [[$$\begin{align*}\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1|X=\text{x}_i)}&=\frac{\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i|Y_i=1)}\times\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)}}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i)}\\ &\propto \color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i|Y_i=1)}\times\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)}.\end{align*}$$]{style="font-size: 90%"}]{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} :::{.vspace style='--space: -30px'} - [**Interpretation:**]{.blue} - $\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)}$: The chance that an email $i$ is a [spam]{.light-red}. - $\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i|Y_i=1)}$: If email $i$ is a [spam]{.light-red}, how likely that its input takes value $\text{x}_i$. - $\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)}$ is **easy** to estimate 😊: $\frac{\text{Number of all Spams}}{\text{Number of total emails}}$. - $\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i|Y_i=1)}$ is **very complicated** to estimate 🥹. ::: ::: ## {visibility="hidden"} ```{python} #| echo: false #| code-fold: true from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde import numpy as np x1 = [1.5, 4.2, 5050] x2 = [1.5, 4.2, 9000] # Given Y = 1 ker_make = gaussian_kde(spam.make[spam.type=="spam"]) ker_address = gaussian_kde(spam.address[spam.type=="spam"]) ker_capital = gaussian_kde(spam.capitalTotal[spam.type=="spam"]) den11 = [ker_make(x1[0]), ker_address(x1[1]), ker_capital(x1[2])] den12 = [ker_make(x2[0]), ker_address(x2[1]), ker_capital(x2[2])] n_spam = np.sum(spam.type=="spam") n_non = spam.shape[0] - n_spam pro11 = n_spam/spam.shape[0] * np.prod(den11) pro12 = n_spam/spam.shape[0] * np.prod(den12) # Given Y = 0 ker_make = gaussian_kde(spam.make[spam.type=="nonspam"]) ker_address = gaussian_kde(spam.address[spam.type=="nonspam"]) ker_capital = gaussian_kde(spam.capitalTotal[spam.type=="nonspam"]) den01 = [ker_make(x1[0]), ker_address(x1[1]), ker_capital(x1[2])] den02 = [ker_make(x2[0]), ker_address(x2[1]), ker_capital(x2[2])] pro01 = n_non/spam.shape[0] * np.prod(den01) pro02 = n_non/spam.shape[0] * np.prod(den02) pro01, pro11 = pro01/(pro01+pro11), pro11/(pro01+pro11) pro02, pro12 = pro02/(pro02+pro12), pro12/(pro02+pro12) ``` - Type of $\text{x}_1=(1.5, 4.2, \color{red}{5050})$ and $\text{x}_2=(1.5, 4.2, \color{blue}{9000})$? --- ### Main assumption & key quantity in NBC ::: {.callout-tip} ### Main assumption of NBC - Within any class $k\in\{1,0\}$, the components of input $X|Y=k$ are [**indpendent**]{.blue} i.e., [$$\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}|Y=k)}=\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=k).$$]{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} ::: ::: {.callout-tip .fragment} ### Key quantity in NBC - From above, the classification probability is computed by [$$\mathbb{P}(Y=1|X=\text{x})\propto \color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y=1)}\color{red}{\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=1)},$$]{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} ::: --- ### Main assumption & key quantity in NBC :::{.callout-tip} ### Key quantity in NBC - From above, the classification probability is computed by [$$\mathbb{P}(Y=1|X=\text{x})\propto \color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y=1)}\color{red}{\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=1)},$$]{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} ::: ::: {style="font-size: 75%"} - [${ }^{\small\text{📚}}$]{style="font-size: 80%"} $\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=1)}$ is just a 1D distribution that can be estimated: | Type of $X_j$ | Distribution | Graphic | |:--------------|:------------------------|:----------------------| | Qualitative | Bernoulli, Multinomial... | `barplot`, `countplot` | | Quantitative | Gausian, Exponential... | `displot`, `hist`, `density`... | | [$^{\text{📚}}$ [Chapter 4, *Introduction to Statistical Learning with R*, James et al. (2021).](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~fdiebold/NoHesitations/BookAdvanced.pdf)]{.slide-note} ::: --- ### Main assumption & key quantity in NBC ::: {.callout-tip} ### Key quantity in NBC - From above, the classification probability is computed by [$$\mathbb{P}(Y=1|X=\text{x})\propto \color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y=1)}\color{red}{\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=1)}.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 75%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: 'center' import plotly.figure_factory as ff import plotly.express as px from plotly.subplots import make_subplots import plotly.graph_objects as go fig = make_subplots(cols=2, rows=1, subplot_titles=("Exclamation", "CapitalTotal")) temp1 = px.histogram(spam, x='charExclamation', color='type', nbins=10000) temp1.data[0].showlegend=False temp1.data[1].showlegend=False temp2 = px.histogram(spam, x='capitalTotal', color='type', nbins=2) fig.add_trace(temp1.data[0], row=1, col=1) fig.add_trace(temp1.data[1], row=1, col=1) fig.add_trace(temp2.data[0], row=1, col=2) fig.add_trace(temp2.data[1], row=1, col=2) fig.update_yaxes(type='log', row=1, col=1) # fig.update_xaxes(type='log', row=1, col=2) fig.update_layout(width=1000, height=230) fig.show() ``` ::: --- ### $M$-class Naive Bayes Classifier - Suppose the target $y\in\{1,2,...,M\}$. :::{.callout-tip} ### Key quantity - For any $d$-dimensional input $\text{x}$ and $k\in\{1,2,...,M\}$: [$$\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k|X=\text{x})}\propto\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k)}\color{red}{\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=k)}.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} ::: :::{.callout-tip .fragment} ### Classification Rule $$\text{x}\text{ belongs to class }\color{blue}{k^*}\text{ if }\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k^*|X=\text{x})}=\max_{1\leq k\leq M}\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k|X=\text{x})}.$$ ::: # Application {background-color="#15797A"} ## Application ### Email type vs only 3 inputs :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - If $\text{x}=($`make`, `address`, `capitalTotal`$)$. - Test data: $20\%$ of all observations. :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| message: false #| warning: false from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split sns.set(style="white") X_train2, X_test2, y_train2, y_test2 = train_test_split(spam[["make","address", "capitalTotal"]], spam.iloc[:,57], test_size = 0.2, random_state=42) nb2 = GaussianNB() _, ax = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(2,2)) nb2 = nb2.fit(X_train2, y_train2) pred2 = nb2.predict(X_test2) conf2 = confusion_matrix(pred2, y_test2) con_fig2 = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(conf2) pr2 = nb2.predict_proba(X_test2)[:,1] con_fig2.plot(ax=ax) plt.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - [**Accuracy**]{.blue}: proportion of correctly classified emails. [[$$\frac{463+62}{463+62+20+297}\approx 0.624.$$]{style="font-size: 80%"}]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} - Misclassification error: [$$1-\text{accuracy}\approx0.376.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} [⚠️ This depends on the split]{.red .fragment} ::: ::: ::: --- ### Email type vs all inputs :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - Data: $\text{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{57},y\in\{0,1\}$. - Test data: the same $20\%$. :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| message: false #| warning: false X_train1, X_test1, y_train1, y_test1 = train_test_split(spam.iloc[:,:57], spam.iloc[:,57], test_size = 0.2, random_state=42) _, ax = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(3,3)) nb1 = GaussianNB() nb1 = nb1.fit(X_train1, y_train1) pred1 = nb1.predict(X_test1) conf1 = confusion_matrix(pred1, y_test1) con_fig1 = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(conf1) pr1 = nb1.predict_proba(X_test1)[:,1] con_fig1.plot(ax=ax) plt.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{style="font-size: 90%"} - Accuracy: proportion of correctly classified emails. [[$$\frac{365+348}{365+348+11+118}\approx 0.846.$$]{style="font-size: 80%"}]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} - Misclassification error: [$$1-\text{accuracy}\approx 0.154.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} [⚠️ This depends on the split]{.red} ::: ::: ::: --- ### Email type vs Selected Inputs :::{.columns} :::{.column width="60%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - Visualize `type` against inputs can help us filter useful input features. - There are too many features, we can apply statistical method, for example, `ANOVA`. ```{python} from scipy.stats import f_oneway # Initialize list to store selected features selected_features = [] p_values = {} # Get feature column names (excluding the target) feature_columns = [col for col in spam.columns if col != 'type'] # For loop to test each feature for feature in feature_columns: # Get unique classes in target variable classes = spam['type'].unique() # Create groups for ANOVA test groups = [] for class_label in classes: group_data = spam[spam['type'] == class_label][feature] groups.append(group_data) # Perform one-way ANOVA f_stat, p_value = f_oneway(*groups) # Store p-value p_values[feature] = p_value # Select feature if p-value < 1e-15 if p_value < 1e-15: selected_features.append(feature) # Create DataFrame with only selected features and target if selected_features: filtered_data = spam[selected_features] ``` - Number of selected features: `{python} len(selected_features)`. :::{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} ```{python} #| echo: false #| message: false #| warning: false #| fig-align: "center" X_train3, X_test3, y_train3, y_test3 = train_test_split(filtered_data, spam.iloc[:,57], test_size = 0.2, random_state=42) _, ax = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(2.5,2.5)) nb3 = GaussianNB() nb3 = nb2.fit(X_train3, y_train3) pred3 = nb2.predict(X_test3) conf3 = confusion_matrix(pred3, y_test3) con_fig3 = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(conf3) pr3 = nb3.predict_proba(X_test3)[:,1] con_fig3.plot(ax=ax) plt.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="40%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - Accuracy: [[$$\frac{359+350}{359+350+9+124}\approx 0.842.$$]{style="font-size: 80%"}]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} - Misclassification error: [$$1-\text{accuracy}\approx 0.158.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} [⚠️ This depends on the split]{.red} ::: ::: ::: --- ### Pros & Cons of NBC :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-note icon=false} ### Pros :::{style="font-size:95%" .incremental} - Efficiency & simplicity - Less training data requirement - Scalability: works well on large and high-dimensional data - Ability to handle categorical data - Ability to handle missing data - Sometimes, it still works well even thought the assumption of `independence` is violeted. ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-important icon=false .fragment} ### Cons :::{style="font-size:90%" .incremental} - May perform poorly when features are highly correlated due to the violation of `independence` assumption. - May not work well for complex relationship. - Zero probability: when some categories are not presented in some training features. - Continuous features often be modeled using Gaussian distribution, which might not always be appropriate. ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # Imbalanced data ⚠️ {background-color="#15797A"} ## Imbalanced data ⚠️ {.incremental auto-animate=true auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out" auto-animate-delay="0"} :::{.style="font-size:70%"} :::{.columns} - If the data contains $95\%$ `nonspam`, always guessing `nonspam` gives $0.95$ accuracy! - `Accuracy` isn't the right metric for `imbalanced` data! :::{.column width="45%" .fragment} :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} - Confustion matrix: :::{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} ![](./img/conf_mat.jpg){width="350px"} ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="55%" .fragment} :::{style="font-size: 90%"} - $\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{purple}{\text{FP}}}$ - $\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{Tan}{\text{FN}}}$ - $\color{ForestGreen}{\text{F1-score}}=\frac{2.\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}.\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}{\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}+\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}$. - $\color{ForestGreen}{\text{F1-score}}$ balances $\color{purple}{\text{FP}}$ & $\color{Tan}{\text{FN}}.$ ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### F1 score :::{.columns} :::{.column width="40%"} ![](./img/conf_mat.jpg){width="350px"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} :::{style="font-size: 75%"} - $\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{purple}{\text{FP}}}$ - $\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{Tan}{\text{FN}}}$ - $\color{ForestGreen}{\text{F1-score}}=\frac{2.\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}.\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}{\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}+\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}$. ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="60%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true import plotly.graph_objects as go x = np.linspace(0,1,20) y = np.linspace(0,1,20) z1 = [[2*x[i]*y[j]/(x[i]+y[j]) for j in range(len(y))] for i in range(len(x))] z2 = [[(x[i]+y[j])/2 for j in range(len(y))] for i in range(len(x))] camera = dict( eye=dict(x=1.7, y=-1.2, z=1.2) ) fig = go.Figure(go.Surface(x = x, y = y, z = z1, name = "F1-score", colorscale = "Blues", showscale = False)) fig.add_trace(go.Surface(x = x, y = y, z = z2, name = "Average", colorscale = "Electric", showscale = False)) avg = (0.2 + 0.9)/2 f1 = 2*0.2*0.9/(0.2+0.9) fig.add_trace( go.Scatter3d( x = [0.2] * 4, y = [0.9] * 4, z = [0, avg, f1, 1], mode="markers + lines", showlegend=False, marker=dict( color='red', size=5), line=dict(color='red', width=2, dash='dot')) ) fig.update_layout(scene = dict( xaxis_title='Precision', yaxis_title='Recall', zaxis_title='Scores'), title = dict(text="F1-score vs Average", y=0.9, x=0.5, font=dict(size = 30, color = "#1C66B5") ), scene_camera=camera, width = 500, height = 420) fig.show() ``` ::: ::: --- ### Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve :::{.columns} :::{.column width="40%"} ![](./img/conf_mat.jpg){width="350px"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - $\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{purple}{\text{FP}}}$ - $\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{Tan}{\text{FN}}}$ - $\color{ForestGreen}{\text{F1-score}}=\frac{2.\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}.\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}{\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}+\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}$ ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="60%" .fragment} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, RocCurveDisplay from plotly.tools import mpl_to_plotly # Method 2: Using roc_curve and Matplotlib directly y1 = 1*(y_test1 == "spam") fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y1.values, pr1.flatten()) plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--', label='Random Classifier') # Diagonal line plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label='ROC Curve') # Figures fig_full = plt.gcf() pl_1 = mpl_to_plotly(fig_full) pl_1.update_layout(width=500, height=420, title=dict(text="ROC Curve of Full model", font=dict(size=25)), xaxis_title = dict(font=dict(size=20, color = "red")), yaxis_title = dict(text='True Positive Rate (Recall)', font=dict(size=20, color = "#EBB31D")), template='plotly_white') pl_1.show() ``` ::: ::: --- ### Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve :::{.columns} :::{.column width="40%"} ![](./img/conf_mat_roc.jpg){width="350px"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -15px"} ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false} $\bullet$ ROC $=\{($[FPR]{style="color:red"}$_{\delta}$,[TPR]{style="color:#EBB31D;"}$_{\delta}):\delta\in[0,1]\}$.
$\bullet$ [Better]{style="color:#20A011;"} model = [Larger]{style="color:#20A011;"} Area Under the Curve (AUC). ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="60%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y1.values, pr2.flatten()) plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label='ROC Curve') plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--', label='Random Classifier') # Diagonal line # Figures fig_2 = plt.gcf() pl_2 = mpl_to_plotly(fig_2) pl_2.update_layout(width=500, height=420, title=dict(text="ROC Curve of 3-input model", font=dict(size=25)), xaxis_title = dict(font=dict(size=20, color = "red")), yaxis_title = dict(text='True Positive Rate (Recall)', font=dict(size=20, color = "#EBB31D")), template='plotly_white') pl_2.show() ``` ::: ::: --- ### ⚠️ Imbalanced data (Summary) :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.callout-tip} ### Confusion matrix - [Precision]{style="color:purple"}: controlls [FP]{style="color:purple"}. - [Recall]{style="color:#EBB31D;"}: controlls [FN]{style="color:#EBB31D;"}. - [F1-score]{style="color:green"}: ballances the two. ::: ![](./img/conf_mat.jpg){width="350px"} ::: :::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.callout-tip} ### ROC Curve & AUC - ROC Curve: ballances [TPR]{style="color:#EBB31D;"} and [FPR]{style="color:red"}. - Can be used to select $\delta\in [0,1]$. - [Better]{style="color:green"} model = [Larger]{style="color:green"} AUC. ::: ![](./img/conf_mat_roc.jpg){width="350px"} ::: ::: --- ### Summary metrics :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - On imbalanced data, accuracy does not nessarily reflect the performance of a model. - [**Precision**]{style="color:purple"} is used to control the number of false positives. - [**Recall**]{style="color:#EBB31D;"} is used to control the number of false negatives. - [**F1-score**]{style="color:green"} is the harmonic mean that balances [**Precision**]{style="color:purple"} and [**Recall**]{style="color:#EBB31D;"}. - After building the model, one can tune the threshold $\delta$ to control the balance between [**Precision**]{style="color:purple"} and [**Recall**]{style="color:#EBB31D;"} using ROC curve. - **AUC** (Area Under the Curve) is a single metric that summarizes the performance of a model across all thresholds. It highlights how well the model can distinguish between classes at any arbitrary threshold. ::: --- ### ⚠️ Imbalanced data (to explore) :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - **Sampling methods**: - Oversampling: random, SMOTE, SMOTE SVM, ADASYN... - Undersampling: random, new miss, CNN, Tomek Links... - **Weight adjustment methods** (nonparametric) - Tree-based algorithms, $k$-NN, kernel methods... - **Tuning threshold** $\delta$. - **Work with packages that handle imbalanced data**: - [`imbalanced-learn`](https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/), [`PyCaret`](https://pycaret.org/)... - Helpful links: [Geeks for Geeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/handling-imbalanced-data-for-classification/), [Angelleon Collado](https://medium.com/@angelleoncollado/data-sampling-methods-in-machine-learning-17c77bbf0579), [Machine Learning Mastery](https://machinelearningmastery.com/tactics-to-combat-imbalanced-classes-in-your-machine-learning-dataset/)... ::: :::{.center} ## 🥳 It's party time 🥂 {background-image="./img/end_page.jpg" background-opacity="0.3" .unlisted .unnumbered .no-header}

[**Reinforcement Learning:**]{.orange} agents (models) learn to complete tasks by interacting with an env. to maximize rewards. ::: ::: ::: ::: ```{python} # path = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hassothea/MLcourses/main/data/" path = './data/' ``` # Naive Bayes Classifier (NBC) {background-color="#15797A"} ## General notation :::{.columns} :::{.column width="60%"} :::{style="font-size: 78%"} - Consider Email spam dataset [{{< fa envelope >}}]{.blue}: ```{python} #| code-line-numbers: "|1|2|3|4" #| code-fold: false #| output-location: fragment import pandas as pd # Load package 'pandas' and call it 'pd' spam = pd.read_csv(path + "spam.txt", sep=" ") # 'path' in your machine spam = spam.drop(columns=["Id"]) spam.iloc[:3,[0,2,3,-1]] ``` - Input ($\text{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$) & target ($\text{y}\in\mathbb{R}^n$): [$$\text{X}=\begin{pmatrix} x_{1,1} & x_{1,2} & \dots & x_{1,d}\\ {\color{blue}{x_{2,1}}} & {\color{blue}{x_{2,2}}} & \dots & {\color{blue}{x_{2,d}}}\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ x_{n,1} & x_{n,2} & \dots & x_{n,d} \end{pmatrix}\quad \&\quad \text{y}=\begin{pmatrix} y_{1}\\ {\color{blue}{y_{2}}}\\ \vdots\\ y_{n}\end{pmatrix}$$]{style="font-size: 85%"} ::: ::: :::{.column width="40%"} :::{style="font-size: 73%" .fragment} - Example: an **input**: ${\color{blue}{\text{x}_i}}=({\color{blue}{x_{i1}}},{\color{blue}{x_{i2}}},\dots, {\color{blue}{x_{id}}})$: `Bag of words` of email $i$. :::{.incremental .vspace style="--space: -20px"} - **Target** ${\color{blue}{y_i}}\in\{1,0\}$ with
{$1:$ [spam]{.light-red}, $0:$ [nonspam]{.green}}. - If $y_i$ are qualitative, the problem is called [**Classification**]{.blue}. - If $y_i$ are quantitative, the problem is called [**Regression**]{.red}. - Example: [**Classify**]{.blue} if an email is a [spam]{.light-red} or not. ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Binary NBC :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 78%"} - Data shape: `{python} spam.shape`. - Total [missing]{.light-red} values: `{python} int(spam.isna().sum().sum())`. - Total [duplicated rows]{.light-red} `{python} int(spam.duplicated().sum())`. - After removing [duplicates]{.light-red}: ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: center import seaborn as sns import matplotlib.pyplot as plt sns.set(style="whitegrid") _, ax = plt.subplots(1,1,figsize=(3.5,2)) spam.drop_duplicates(inplace=True) sns.countplot( data=spam, x="type", hue="type", stat="percent") ax.set_title("Barplot of Email Type") ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], fmt="%.2f", ) ax.bar_label(ax.containers[1], fmt="%.2f") plt.show() ``` ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - As a human, how would you predict if an email is a spam or not just by looking at its features? - [**Main principal of Binary NBC:**]{.blue} Look at each [**feature marginally**]{.light-blue}, then [**combine the information**]{.light-red} to produce the class probability. - This can be accomplished using [**Bayesian Theorem**]{.blue} + some [**assumption**]{.light-red}. ::: ::: ::: --- ### Model Motivation :::{style="font-size:80%" .incremental} - Given an email (input) $\text{x}_i=(0, 0.64,\dots,278)\in\mathbb{R}^{57}$, how would you guess its type $y_i$? - 🔑 [**The most important quantity**]{.green} in (binary) classification: [$$\boxed{\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1|X=\text{x}_i)}.}$$ [**Interpretation:** Given $\text{x}_i$, how likely that it is in class 1 (spam)?]{.blue}]{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} - [**Decision rule:**]{.blue} [$$\boxed{\text{ Email x}_i\text{ is a spam }\Leftrightarrow\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1|X=\text{x}_i)}\geq 0.5.}$$]{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} - From now, building a **classifier** is trying to estimate this chance [$$\boxed{\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1|X=\text{x}_i)}.}$$]{.vspace style="--space: -15px"} ::: --- ### Recall Bayes's Theorem ::: {.callout-tip} ### Bayes's Theorem :::{.columns} :::{.column width="70%"} For any two events $O,H$ with $\mathbb{P}(O)\times\mathbb{P}(H)>0,$ \begin{equation}\overbrace{\mathbb{P}(H|O)}^{\text{Posterior}}=\frac{\overbrace{\mathbb{P}(O|H)}^{\text{Likelihood}}\times\overbrace{\mathbb{P}(H)}^{\text{Prior}}}{\underbrace{\mathbb{P}(O)}_{\text{Marginal}}}.\end{equation} :::{style="font-size: 85%"} - $\mathbb{P}(H)$: Prior belief of having hypothesis $H$. - $\mathbb{P}(O|H)$: If $H$ is true, how likely for $O$ to be observed? - $\mathbb{P}(H|O)$: If $O$ is observed, how likely for $H$ to be true? - $\mathbb{P}(O)$: How likely for $O$ to be observed in general? ::: ::: :::{.column width="30%"} ![](./img/diagram.png){width="180"} :::{.vspace style='--space: -20px'} [![](./img/Thomas.png){width="170"}](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Bayes){target="_blank"} ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### Model Setting :::{style="font-size:85%" .incremental} - Bayes's theorem implies: [[$$\begin{align*}\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1|X=\text{x}_i)}&=\frac{\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i|Y_i=1)}\times\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)}}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i)}\\ &\propto \color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i|Y_i=1)}\times\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)}.\end{align*}$$]{style="font-size: 90%"}]{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} :::{.vspace style='--space: -30px'} - [**Interpretation:**]{.blue} - $\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)}$: The chance that an email $i$ is a [spam]{.light-red}. - $\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i|Y_i=1)}$: If email $i$ is a [spam]{.light-red}, how likely that its input takes value $\text{x}_i$. - $\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)}$ is **easy** to estimate 😊: $\frac{\text{Number of all Spams}}{\text{Number of total emails}}$. - $\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}_i|Y_i=1)}$ is **very complicated** to estimate 🥹. ::: ::: ## {visibility="hidden"} ```{python} #| echo: false #| code-fold: true from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde import numpy as np x1 = [1.5, 4.2, 5050] x2 = [1.5, 4.2, 9000] # Given Y = 1 ker_make = gaussian_kde(spam.make[spam.type=="spam"]) ker_address = gaussian_kde(spam.address[spam.type=="spam"]) ker_capital = gaussian_kde(spam.capitalTotal[spam.type=="spam"]) den11 = [ker_make(x1[0]), ker_address(x1[1]), ker_capital(x1[2])] den12 = [ker_make(x2[0]), ker_address(x2[1]), ker_capital(x2[2])] n_spam = np.sum(spam.type=="spam") n_non = spam.shape[0] - n_spam pro11 = n_spam/spam.shape[0] * np.prod(den11) pro12 = n_spam/spam.shape[0] * np.prod(den12) # Given Y = 0 ker_make = gaussian_kde(spam.make[spam.type=="nonspam"]) ker_address = gaussian_kde(spam.address[spam.type=="nonspam"]) ker_capital = gaussian_kde(spam.capitalTotal[spam.type=="nonspam"]) den01 = [ker_make(x1[0]), ker_address(x1[1]), ker_capital(x1[2])] den02 = [ker_make(x2[0]), ker_address(x2[1]), ker_capital(x2[2])] pro01 = n_non/spam.shape[0] * np.prod(den01) pro02 = n_non/spam.shape[0] * np.prod(den02) pro01, pro11 = pro01/(pro01+pro11), pro11/(pro01+pro11) pro02, pro12 = pro02/(pro02+pro12), pro12/(pro02+pro12) ``` - Type of $\text{x}_1=(1.5, 4.2, \color{red}{5050})$ and $\text{x}_2=(1.5, 4.2, \color{blue}{9000})$? --- ### Main assumption & key quantity in NBC ::: {.callout-tip} ### Main assumption of NBC - Within any class $k\in\{1,0\}$, the components of input $X|Y=k$ are [**indpendent**]{.blue} i.e., [$$\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X=\text{x}|Y=k)}=\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=k).$$]{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} ::: ::: {.callout-tip .fragment} ### Key quantity in NBC - From above, the classification probability is computed by [$$\mathbb{P}(Y=1|X=\text{x})\propto \color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y=1)}\color{red}{\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=1)},$$]{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} ::: --- ### Main assumption & key quantity in NBC :::{.callout-tip} ### Key quantity in NBC - From above, the classification probability is computed by [$$\mathbb{P}(Y=1|X=\text{x})\propto \color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y=1)}\color{red}{\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=1)},$$]{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} ::: ::: {style="font-size: 75%"} - [${ }^{\small\text{📚}}$]{style="font-size: 80%"} $\color{red}{\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=1)}$ is just a 1D distribution that can be estimated: | Type of $X_j$ | Distribution | Graphic | |:--------------|:------------------------|:----------------------| | Qualitative | Bernoulli, Multinomial... | `barplot`, `countplot` | | Quantitative | Gausian, Exponential... | `displot`, `hist`, `density`... | | [$^{\text{📚}}$ [Chapter 4, *Introduction to Statistical Learning with R*, James et al. (2021).](https://www.sas.upenn.edu/~fdiebold/NoHesitations/BookAdvanced.pdf)]{.slide-note} ::: --- ### Main assumption & key quantity in NBC ::: {.callout-tip} ### Key quantity in NBC - From above, the classification probability is computed by [$$\mathbb{P}(Y=1|X=\text{x})\propto \color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y=1)}\color{red}{\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=1)}.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 75%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| fig-align: 'center' import plotly.figure_factory as ff import plotly.express as px from plotly.subplots import make_subplots import plotly.graph_objects as go fig = make_subplots(cols=2, rows=1, subplot_titles=("Exclamation", "CapitalTotal")) temp1 = px.histogram(spam, x='charExclamation', color='type', nbins=10000) temp1.data[0].showlegend=False temp1.data[1].showlegend=False temp2 = px.histogram(spam, x='capitalTotal', color='type', nbins=2) fig.add_trace(temp1.data[0], row=1, col=1) fig.add_trace(temp1.data[1], row=1, col=1) fig.add_trace(temp2.data[0], row=1, col=2) fig.add_trace(temp2.data[1], row=1, col=2) fig.update_yaxes(type='log', row=1, col=1) # fig.update_xaxes(type='log', row=1, col=2) fig.update_layout(width=1000, height=230) fig.show() ``` ::: --- ### $M$-class Naive Bayes Classifier - Suppose the target $y\in\{1,2,...,M\}$. :::{.callout-tip} ### Key quantity - For any $d$-dimensional input $\text{x}$ and $k\in\{1,2,...,M\}$: [$$\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k|X=\text{x})}\propto\color{green}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k)}\color{red}{\prod_{j=1}^d\mathbb{P}(X_j=x_j|Y=k)}.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} ::: :::{.callout-tip .fragment} ### Classification Rule $$\text{x}\text{ belongs to class }\color{blue}{k^*}\text{ if }\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k^*|X=\text{x})}=\max_{1\leq k\leq M}\color{blue}{\mathbb{P}(Y=k|X=\text{x})}.$$ ::: # Application {background-color="#15797A"} ## Application ### Email type vs only 3 inputs :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - If $\text{x}=($`make`, `address`, `capitalTotal`$)$. - Test data: $20\%$ of all observations. :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| message: false #| warning: false from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split sns.set(style="white") X_train2, X_test2, y_train2, y_test2 = train_test_split(spam[["make","address", "capitalTotal"]], spam.iloc[:,57], test_size = 0.2, random_state=42) nb2 = GaussianNB() _, ax = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(2,2)) nb2 = nb2.fit(X_train2, y_train2) pred2 = nb2.predict(X_test2) conf2 = confusion_matrix(pred2, y_test2) con_fig2 = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(conf2) pr2 = nb2.predict_proba(X_test2)[:,1] con_fig2.plot(ax=ax) plt.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - [**Accuracy**]{.blue}: proportion of correctly classified emails. [[$$\frac{463+62}{463+62+20+297}\approx 0.624.$$]{style="font-size: 80%"}]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} - Misclassification error: [$$1-\text{accuracy}\approx0.376.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} [⚠️ This depends on the split]{.red .fragment} ::: ::: ::: --- ### Email type vs all inputs :::{.columns} :::{.column width="55%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - Data: $\text{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{57},y\in\{0,1\}$. - Test data: the same $20\%$. :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true #| message: false #| warning: false X_train1, X_test1, y_train1, y_test1 = train_test_split(spam.iloc[:,:57], spam.iloc[:,57], test_size = 0.2, random_state=42) _, ax = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(3,3)) nb1 = GaussianNB() nb1 = nb1.fit(X_train1, y_train1) pred1 = nb1.predict(X_test1) conf1 = confusion_matrix(pred1, y_test1) con_fig1 = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(conf1) pr1 = nb1.predict_proba(X_test1)[:,1] con_fig1.plot(ax=ax) plt.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="45%"} :::{style="font-size: 90%"} - Accuracy: proportion of correctly classified emails. [[$$\frac{365+348}{365+348+11+118}\approx 0.846.$$]{style="font-size: 80%"}]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} - Misclassification error: [$$1-\text{accuracy}\approx 0.154.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} [⚠️ This depends on the split]{.red} ::: ::: ::: --- ### Email type vs Selected Inputs :::{.columns} :::{.column width="60%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - Visualize `type` against inputs can help us filter useful input features. - There are too many features, we can apply statistical method, for example, `ANOVA`. ```{python} from scipy.stats import f_oneway # Initialize list to store selected features selected_features = [] p_values = {} # Get feature column names (excluding the target) feature_columns = [col for col in spam.columns if col != 'type'] # For loop to test each feature for feature in feature_columns: # Get unique classes in target variable classes = spam['type'].unique() # Create groups for ANOVA test groups = [] for class_label in classes: group_data = spam[spam['type'] == class_label][feature] groups.append(group_data) # Perform one-way ANOVA f_stat, p_value = f_oneway(*groups) # Store p-value p_values[feature] = p_value # Select feature if p-value < 1e-15 if p_value < 1e-15: selected_features.append(feature) # Create DataFrame with only selected features and target if selected_features: filtered_data = spam[selected_features] ``` - Number of selected features: `{python} len(selected_features)`. :::{.vspace style="--space: -20px"} ```{python} #| echo: false #| message: false #| warning: false #| fig-align: "center" X_train3, X_test3, y_train3, y_test3 = train_test_split(filtered_data, spam.iloc[:,57], test_size = 0.2, random_state=42) _, ax = plt.subplots(1,1, figsize=(2.5,2.5)) nb3 = GaussianNB() nb3 = nb2.fit(X_train3, y_train3) pred3 = nb2.predict(X_test3) conf3 = confusion_matrix(pred3, y_test3) con_fig3 = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(conf3) pr3 = nb3.predict_proba(X_test3)[:,1] con_fig3.plot(ax=ax) plt.show() ``` ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="40%"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - Accuracy: [[$$\frac{359+350}{359+350+9+124}\approx 0.842.$$]{style="font-size: 80%"}]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} - Misclassification error: [$$1-\text{accuracy}\approx 0.158.$$]{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} [⚠️ This depends on the split]{.red} ::: ::: ::: --- ### Pros & Cons of NBC :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-note icon=false} ### Pros :::{style="font-size:95%" .incremental} - Efficiency & simplicity - Less training data requirement - Scalability: works well on large and high-dimensional data - Ability to handle categorical data - Ability to handle missing data - Sometimes, it still works well even thought the assumption of `independence` is violeted. ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="50%"} :::{.callout-important icon=false .fragment} ### Cons :::{style="font-size:90%" .incremental} - May perform poorly when features are highly correlated due to the violation of `independence` assumption. - May not work well for complex relationship. - Zero probability: when some categories are not presented in some training features. - Continuous features often be modeled using Gaussian distribution, which might not always be appropriate. ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: # Imbalanced data ⚠️ {background-color="#15797A"} ## Imbalanced data ⚠️ {.incremental auto-animate=true auto-animate-easing="ease-in-out" auto-animate-delay="0"} :::{.style="font-size:70%"} :::{.columns} - If the data contains $95\%$ `nonspam`, always guessing `nonspam` gives $0.95$ accuracy! - `Accuracy` isn't the right metric for `imbalanced` data! :::{.column width="45%" .fragment} :::{.vspace style="--space: -10px"} - Confustion matrix: :::{.vspace style="--space: -30px"} ![](./img/conf_mat.jpg){width="350px"} ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="55%" .fragment} :::{style="font-size: 90%"} - $\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{purple}{\text{FP}}}$ - $\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{Tan}{\text{FN}}}$ - $\color{ForestGreen}{\text{F1-score}}=\frac{2.\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}.\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}{\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}+\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}$. - $\color{ForestGreen}{\text{F1-score}}$ balances $\color{purple}{\text{FP}}$ & $\color{Tan}{\text{FN}}.$ ::: ::: ::: ::: --- ### F1 score :::{.columns} :::{.column width="40%"} ![](./img/conf_mat.jpg){width="350px"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} :::{style="font-size: 75%"} - $\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{purple}{\text{FP}}}$ - $\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{Tan}{\text{FN}}}$ - $\color{ForestGreen}{\text{F1-score}}=\frac{2.\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}.\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}{\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}+\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}$. ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="60%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true import plotly.graph_objects as go x = np.linspace(0,1,20) y = np.linspace(0,1,20) z1 = [[2*x[i]*y[j]/(x[i]+y[j]) for j in range(len(y))] for i in range(len(x))] z2 = [[(x[i]+y[j])/2 for j in range(len(y))] for i in range(len(x))] camera = dict( eye=dict(x=1.7, y=-1.2, z=1.2) ) fig = go.Figure(go.Surface(x = x, y = y, z = z1, name = "F1-score", colorscale = "Blues", showscale = False)) fig.add_trace(go.Surface(x = x, y = y, z = z2, name = "Average", colorscale = "Electric", showscale = False)) avg = (0.2 + 0.9)/2 f1 = 2*0.2*0.9/(0.2+0.9) fig.add_trace( go.Scatter3d( x = [0.2] * 4, y = [0.9] * 4, z = [0, avg, f1, 1], mode="markers + lines", showlegend=False, marker=dict( color='red', size=5), line=dict(color='red', width=2, dash='dot')) ) fig.update_layout(scene = dict( xaxis_title='Precision', yaxis_title='Recall', zaxis_title='Scores'), title = dict(text="F1-score vs Average", y=0.9, x=0.5, font=dict(size = 30, color = "#1C66B5") ), scene_camera=camera, width = 500, height = 420) fig.show() ``` ::: ::: --- ### Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve :::{.columns} :::{.column width="40%"} ![](./img/conf_mat.jpg){width="350px"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -25px"} :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - $\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{purple}{\text{FP}}}$ - $\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}=\frac{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}}{\color{CornflowerBlue}{\text{TP}}+\color{Tan}{\text{FN}}}$ - $\color{ForestGreen}{\text{F1-score}}=\frac{2.\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}.\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}{\color{purple}{\text{Precision}}+\color{Tan}{\text{Recall}}}$ ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="60%" .fragment} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, RocCurveDisplay from plotly.tools import mpl_to_plotly # Method 2: Using roc_curve and Matplotlib directly y1 = 1*(y_test1 == "spam") fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y1.values, pr1.flatten()) plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--', label='Random Classifier') # Diagonal line plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label='ROC Curve') # Figures fig_full = plt.gcf() pl_1 = mpl_to_plotly(fig_full) pl_1.update_layout(width=500, height=420, title=dict(text="ROC Curve of Full model", font=dict(size=25)), xaxis_title = dict(font=dict(size=20, color = "red")), yaxis_title = dict(text='True Positive Rate (Recall)', font=dict(size=20, color = "#EBB31D")), template='plotly_white') pl_1.show() ``` ::: ::: --- ### Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve :::{.columns} :::{.column width="40%"} ![](./img/conf_mat_roc.jpg){width="350px"} :::{.vspace style="--space: -15px"} ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon=false} $\bullet$ ROC $=\{($[FPR]{style="color:red"}$_{\delta}$,[TPR]{style="color:#EBB31D;"}$_{\delta}):\delta\in[0,1]\}$.
$\bullet$ [Better]{style="color:#20A011;"} model = [Larger]{style="color:#20A011;"} Area Under the Curve (AUC). ::: ::: ::: :::{.column width="60%"} ```{python} #| echo: true #| code-fold: true fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y1.values, pr2.flatten()) plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label='ROC Curve') plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], 'k--', label='Random Classifier') # Diagonal line # Figures fig_2 = plt.gcf() pl_2 = mpl_to_plotly(fig_2) pl_2.update_layout(width=500, height=420, title=dict(text="ROC Curve of 3-input model", font=dict(size=25)), xaxis_title = dict(font=dict(size=20, color = "red")), yaxis_title = dict(text='True Positive Rate (Recall)', font=dict(size=20, color = "#EBB31D")), template='plotly_white') pl_2.show() ``` ::: ::: --- ### ⚠️ Imbalanced data (Summary) :::{.columns} :::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.callout-tip} ### Confusion matrix - [Precision]{style="color:purple"}: controlls [FP]{style="color:purple"}. - [Recall]{style="color:#EBB31D;"}: controlls [FN]{style="color:#EBB31D;"}. - [F1-score]{style="color:green"}: ballances the two. ::: ![](./img/conf_mat.jpg){width="350px"} ::: :::{.column width="50%"} ::: {.callout-tip} ### ROC Curve & AUC - ROC Curve: ballances [TPR]{style="color:#EBB31D;"} and [FPR]{style="color:red"}. - Can be used to select $\delta\in [0,1]$. - [Better]{style="color:green"} model = [Larger]{style="color:green"} AUC. ::: ![](./img/conf_mat_roc.jpg){width="350px"} ::: ::: --- ### Summary metrics :::{style="font-size: 80%" .incremental} - On imbalanced data, accuracy does not nessarily reflect the performance of a model. - [**Precision**]{style="color:purple"} is used to control the number of false positives. - [**Recall**]{style="color:#EBB31D;"} is used to control the number of false negatives. - [**F1-score**]{style="color:green"} is the harmonic mean that balances [**Precision**]{style="color:purple"} and [**Recall**]{style="color:#EBB31D;"}. - After building the model, one can tune the threshold $\delta$ to control the balance between [**Precision**]{style="color:purple"} and [**Recall**]{style="color:#EBB31D;"} using ROC curve. - **AUC** (Area Under the Curve) is a single metric that summarizes the performance of a model across all thresholds. It highlights how well the model can distinguish between classes at any arbitrary threshold. ::: --- ### ⚠️ Imbalanced data (to explore) :::{style="font-size: 80%"} - **Sampling methods**: - Oversampling: random, SMOTE, SMOTE SVM, ADASYN... - Undersampling: random, new miss, CNN, Tomek Links... - **Weight adjustment methods** (nonparametric) - Tree-based algorithms, $k$-NN, kernel methods... - **Tuning threshold** $\delta$. - **Work with packages that handle imbalanced data**: - [`imbalanced-learn`](https://imbalanced-learn.org/stable/), [`PyCaret`](https://pycaret.org/)... - Helpful links: [Geeks for Geeks](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/handling-imbalanced-data-for-classification/), [Angelleon Collado](https://medium.com/@angelleoncollado/data-sampling-methods-in-machine-learning-17c77bbf0579), [Machine Learning Mastery](https://machinelearningmastery.com/tactics-to-combat-imbalanced-classes-in-your-machine-learning-dataset/)... ::: :::{.center} ## 🥳 It's party time 🥂 {background-image="./img/end_page.jpg" background-opacity="0.3" .unlisted .unnumbered .no-header}
